title: So close to Moscow, and no closer

facts.text: On the morning of 2 December 1941 Field Marshal Fedor von Bock, commanding Army Group Centre, told his generals that the Red Army was close to breaking. Later that day he told the army chief of staff, General Franz Halder, that "doubts of success are beginning to take definite form."

He blamed declining strength, the cold and stiffening resistance. Only the day before he had sent the army high command a teletype saying the belief in an impending Soviet collapse had proved "a phantasy" and that the offensive had lost "all sense and purpose."
The stakes were already huge. By 1 November the German army had lost 686,000 men in the east, a fifth of all it had committed, and its panzer divisions were down to 35 percent of their tanks.

The closest German approach to Moscow is often given as Khimki, a northwestern suburb about 19 miles (30 km) from the Kremlin, where a German reconnaissance unit is said to have arrived on 2 December.

That story is shaky. Accounts disagree on the date (2, 4 or 5 December) and on the unit, often named as the 62nd Pioneer Battalion, and Russian researchers say no wartime document of such a raid has ever been published.
Much of it traces to the 1963 bestseller on the Russian campaign by Paul Carell, the pen name of Paul Karl Schmidt, who had been press chief of Hitler's Foreign Ministry.
The best known detail, that German soldiers saw the spires of the Kremlin from Khimki, is a legend. No solid source supports it.

The documented high water mark lies just to the north. By 28 November the 2nd Panzer Division had come almost to a standstill west of Krasnaya Polyana, about twelve miles north of Moscow, against minefields and earthworks ringing the city.

For two weeks the temperature had ranged between 0 and 20 degrees Fahrenheit. On the morning of 4 December, after heavy snow, it stood at 4 below zero, and Bock noted in his diary that it was "icy cold."

Winter clothing never reached most of the men. As early as November it was being left in storage because it could not be moved forward without cutting off other supplies, and weeks later a third of it had still not been issued.
Bock's doubts proved right. Within days his panzer groups were pulling back from Krasnaya Polyana, and on 19 December he handed over his command and went on sick leave.

declassified.fact: There was one real surprise breakthrough that week. On 1 December the German 258th Infantry Division broke through the Soviet line south of the Moscow to Smolensk highway, to the surprise of both sides. By the afternoon of 3 December it was fighting its way back west out of an encirclement.

body:
Field Marshal Fedor von Bock told his generals the Red Army was close to breaking. By that evening he was admitting his own doubts.

2 December 1941. The day before, Bock had warned the high command that the belief in a Soviet collapse had proved "a phantasy." Now he told General Halder that "doubts of success are beginning to take definite form."

This is also the date often given for a German patrol reaching Khimki, 19 miles from the Kremlin, and seeing its spires. Much of that story traces to a 1963 bestseller by a former press chief of Hitler's Foreign Ministry. No solid source supports the spires.

The documented high water mark lay near Krasnaya Polyana, about twelve miles north of Moscow. Within days Bock's panzer groups were pulling back.
